callout.text: Waiters kept it all in their heads

storyboard.claim: Vienna waiters tracked complex table orders purely from memory.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A cafe with a waiter holding a pad, tracking table orders from memory.
storyboard.onScreenText: Waiters kept it all in their heads
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the Zeigarnik story with a concrete 1920s cafe scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the mental load of holding many orders without writing anything down.

callout.text: Keeping it all in their heads

storyboard.claim: Watching the waiters is impressive: they hold every detail mentally.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A surprised onlooker reacting to the waiters' memory feat in the cafe.
storyboard.onScreenText: Keeping it all in their heads
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reaction to the cafe scene just introduced.
storyboard.addedInformation: Specifies the detail: who ordered the schnitzel and who ordered black coffee.

storyboard.claim: Once the table is settled, the waiters' memory of the order is wiped clean.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A blank-faced figure holding a notes pad after the order is finished.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the cafe scene: the memory is dumped after payment.
storyboard.addedInformation: The memory is released the moment the transaction ends.

callout.text: Five minutes later, it is forgotten

storyboard.claim: Five minutes later the waiters no longer remember the orders; the brain lets go.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An emptied-out figure in the cafe, nothing held, showing the lost detail.
storyboard.onScreenText: Five minutes later, it is forgotten
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the wiped memory with the time gap.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the Zeigarnik finding: the brain struggles to let go of incomplete tasks.

storyboard.claim: An unfinished goal stays active in working memory and produces intrusive thoughts.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-step flow from unfinished goal to working memory to intrusive thoughts.
storyboard.onScreenText: Unfinished goal, working memory, intrusive thoughts
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The Zeigarnik mechanism is now stated as a cause chain.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the cause-effect sequence the viewer can follow without sound.

storyboard.claim: A seventy-item to-do list makes the brain treat each item like an unpaid restaurant bill.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried figure slumped over a long list of notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the restaurant-bill image to the modern to-do list.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the mental cost of unfinished items concrete: each one keeps asking to be settled.

callout.text: Seventy tabs open in your head

storyboard.claim: The unfinished list runs constantly in the background, a low hum of anxiety, like many open browser tabs.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried figure looking at a phone, a stand-in for many open tabs.
storyboard.onScreenText: Seventy tabs open in your head
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Switches the image from restaurant bills to browser tabs.
storyboard.addedInformation: Explains the cost in terms of working memory: each open item draws on the same limited resource.

storyboard.claim: Even one open task is slowed down by the other 69 running in the background.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A slumped, worried figure, drained by the many open items.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the tab analogy: one tab is affected by all the rest.
storyboard.addedInformation: Says the drain is battery-like and eventually a full crash.

storyboard.claim: If the list crashes the brain, the question is what the successful people use instead.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure thinking through the problem of tracking tasks without a list.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivots from the diagnosis to the solution.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the calendar as the replacement for the list.

storyboard.claim: Successful people abandon the to-do list and move everything onto a calendar.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A decisive figure pointing toward a clock, the calendar as schedule time.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with the calendar method.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the switch as a full replacement, not an add-on.

storyboard.claim: The calendar is the exclusive blueprint for reality: everything gets scheduled.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure pointing firmly at a calendar blueprint on the wall.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Expands the calendar rule from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the rule exclusive: nothing is kept outside the calendar.

storyboard.claim: Anything that needs doing receives its own dedicated time block.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure talking about a single block of time on a schedule.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the first example, an entrepreneur who blocks everything.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the unit of scheduling: each task gets a block, not a list line.

storyboard.claim: Even thirty minutes of scrolling Twitter and LinkedIn is put on the calendar.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure holding a smartphone, the scrolling habit made into a scheduled block.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the concrete example of the entrepreneur's schedule.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the rule applies even to leisure and social media, not only work.

storyboard.claim: Processing the inbox for 45 minutes and catching up with assistants both go on the schedule.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure pointing at a schedule that includes inbox and assistant time.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds more of the same entrepreneur's routine.
storyboard.addedInformation: Confirms the scheduling covers administrative work as well.

storyboard.claim: His cardinal rule: anything not scheduled does not get done and does not exist.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure pointing firmly, stating the rule.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Summarizes the entrepreneur's rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: Turns scheduling into the only test of whether a task is real.

storyboard.claim: The CEO schedules his whole life in fifteen-minute blocks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure talking about a fifteen-minute block schedule.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the second, more extreme example.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the granularity: even short tasks get a fifteen-minute slot.

storyboard.claim: Office hours are four fifteen-minute blocks a week; outside them he is unreachable.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A closed door as the boundary of the office-hours blocks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the CEO example with office hours.
storyboard.addedInformation: The door shows the exclusion: access only inside the blocks.

storyboard.claim: Placing a task on the calendar neutralizes the Zeigarnik effect.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A relieved figure pointing at a scheduled slot.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the neuroscience: the calendar fixes the loop.
storyboard.addedInformation: Connects the calendar method directly to the brain mechanism.

storyboard.claim: A scheduled time closes the loop, like paying the waiter's bill.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure holding a wallet, the metaphor of settling a bill.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the cafe bill image to explain the calendar effect.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the closing of the loop concrete: a fixed time settles the item.

storyboard.claim: A locked time such as Thursday at 4:30 stops the brain from nagging about the errand.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure thinking beside a clock showing a specific scheduled time.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the concrete example of a locked-in time.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the specificity needed: a day and a time, not just a task.

callout.text: The plan lives on a hard drive

storyboard.claim: The calendar offloads cognitive burden from fragile working memory onto an external store.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure holding a phone, the calendar as external storage.
storyboard.onScreenText: The plan lives on a hard drive
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Finishes the sentence from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the calendar as a memory device outside the head.

storyboard.claim: The listener objects: blocking out an entire life in fifteen-minute increments feels excessive.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A skeptical, worried figure thinking over the idea.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the pushback section.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the objection that the method may be too rigid.

storyboard.claim: The critic says a scheduled life sounds like a self-imposed prison.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Chains as a bound, imprisoned reading, with a worried figure beside them.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the objection with the prison image.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the feared cost: freedom given up to the schedule.

storyboard.claim: A friend invites you for coffee on a Tuesday, and you have to refuse because of the blocks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure holding a phone, talking as if answering a call from a friend.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the concrete scenario behind the objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the social cost of rigid scheduling.

storyboard.claim: Rigid scheduling is not success; the rigid constraint actually creates freedom.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure pointing, answering the objection.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the friend-invite objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reframes the constraint as the source of freedom.

storyboard.claim: Operating off a massive to-do list leaves you perpetually time bankrupt.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried figure slumped under a long list.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Counter-argument for the calendar method, after the objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the to-do list, not the calendar, as the real time drain.

storyboard.claim: Even during coffee with a friend you agonize over the work you are not doing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried figure thinking, distracted from the moment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the emotional cost of the list in a social setting.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows that the list keeps you from being present, not just tired.

storyboard.claim: A list-driven life means you are not present with the people around you.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried, distracted figure holding a phone instead of looking up.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the guilt argument into presence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Contrasts with the calendar life, which holds work, gym and family time.

storyboard.claim: With a calendar you can see a specific block, such as write proposal, and know where you stand.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure holding notes and pointing at a scheduled block.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives a concrete calendar block in the friend-invite scenario.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the calendar gives a clear picture of current commitments.

storyboard.claim: If the block can move without breaking the deadline, you go to coffee with zero guilt and are fully present.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A relieved, happy figure talking about moving the block.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the coffee scenario from the calendar side.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the decision test: move the block only if the deadline allows it.

callout.text: The to-do list hides the truth

storyboard.claim: The calendar reflects your actual capacity; a to-do list lets you lie to yourself about time.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A clock laid over a calendar, showing the real capacity behind the to-do list.
storyboard.onScreenText: The to-do list hides the truth
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reframes the calendar as honest, not restrictive.
storyboard.addedInformation: Says the to-do list hides how little time there is.

storyboard.claim: A list can always take one more line, but a calendar is bound by physics: two blocks of time cannot overlap.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure holding notes, pointing at a fixed time layout.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the calendar is more honest than the list.
storyboard.addedInformation: Adds the hard limit of physical time that a paper list lacks.

storyboard.claim: The calendar forces you to confront reality and the friction of choice.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A figure thinking hard about the limit of time.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows from the physics of time blocks.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the friction of choice as the benefit.

storyboard.claim: Allocating time is a decision problem: with 70 items and room for 10, the rest must be cut.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter with two buckets: items that fit the calendar and items cut from the list.
storyboard.onScreenText: Fits the calendar, Cut from the list
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the decision problem into a sorting structure.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the arithmetic of choice: most items do not fit.

storyboard.claim: Sixty things must be cut, and making cuts takes the hardest professional skill: saying no.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried figure slumped, facing the cuts.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the sorter with the number of cuts.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the skill needed: the ability to say no.

storyboard.claim: A parent in the kitchen is trying to untangle a chaotic family schedule while cooking dinner.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried parent thinking in a kitchen beside a cooking pot.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Puts a human face on the saying-no problem.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets the everyday scene: a normal Tuesday with activities to coordinate.

storyboard.claim: A text arrives from the PTA president asking for help.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried parent holding a buzzing smartphone in the kitchen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The request arrives in the kitchen scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: Identifies the request source: the school PTA president.

storyboard.claim: The PTA asks the parent to chair the fundraising committee, and the reaction is profound guilt.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried parent holding the phone, reading the request.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Quotes the request directly.
storyboard.addedInformation: The request is for a specific role, the spring fundraising committee chair.

storyboard.claim: The parent has zero capacity: already sleeping six hours a night with stress through the roof.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A slumped, exhausted parent in the kitchen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The inner monologue about the request.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the concrete evidence of low capacity: six hours of sleep.

storyboard.claim: Saying no feels like letting the school down, so the parent feels forced to say yes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A worried parent thinking, torn between the request and the limit.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the guilt-driven internal monologue.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the fear of judgment from other parents, which drives the yes.
